title: Naming binary compounds
competency: Name binary compounds from their formulas.

keywords.def: A compound made of only two different elements.

en.text: Name the metal first with its element name. Then name the non-metal with the ending -ide: oxygen becomes oxide, chlorine becomes chloride. For metals with more than one valence, write the valence in Roman numerals: FeCl₃ is iron (III) chloride.

screens.title: Fix the name
screens.ask: A student named a compound of calcium and sulfur "sulfur calcium". What is the correct name?
screens.after: The metal comes first, and sulfur takes the ending -ide. The name is calcium sulfide.

screens.title: 3.2.5 Naming binary compounds
paras: In naming a compound, the metal is named first.
A binary compound is made of only two different elements, in a whole number ratio.

screens.title: Rule 1
paras: The metal keeps its element name.
The end of the non-metal name changes to -ide.

screens.title: Rule 1 example: naming KBr
steps: K is potassium, a metal. Name it first.

screens.title: Rule 2
paras: Some metals form more than one positive ion.
Write the valence in Roman numerals in brackets.
Fe²⁺ is iron (II), read "iron two". Fe³⁺ is iron (III), read "iron three".

screens.title: Rule 2 example: naming Fe₂O₃
steps: Fe is iron. Iron has two valences, so we need a Roman numeral.
O has valence 2. Three O atoms give 3 × 2 = 6.
Two Fe atoms share 6, so each Fe has 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
Write 3 as III in brackets: iron (III).
Oxygen becomes oxide. Fe₂O₃ is iron (III) oxide.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A compound made of only two different elements.

screens.why:
Mg is magnesium, the metal: it comes first.
O is oxygen, the non-metal.
Oxygen's ending changes to -ide: oxide.
Answer: magnesium oxide.
Molybdenum is a different element (Mo).

screens.title: Non-metal name in a compound
screens.why:
Keep the start of the non-metal's name and add -ide.
Nitrogen → nitride. Oxygen → oxide.
Chlorine → chloride. Sulfur → sulfide.
Iodine → iodide.
screens.clue: Keep the start of the name, add -ide.
screens.text: Match each non-metal to its name in a compound.

screens.why:
Ag is silver, the metal: it comes first.
Cl is chlorine, the non-metal.
Chlorine changes to chloride.
Answer: silver chloride.

screens.text: Name the compound FeS. (S has valence 2.)
screens.why:
Iron has two valences, so the name needs a Roman numeral.
One S has valence 2.
One Fe must match it, so iron has valence 2.
Write iron (II), then sulfur → sulfide.
Answer: iron (II) sulfide. The numeral goes right after iron.
screens.clue: Work out iron's valence from sulfur.

screens.why:
Each Cl has valence 1.
Three Cl give 3 × 1 = 3.
One Fe must match 3, so iron has valence 3: iron (III).
Chlorine becomes chloride.
Answer: iron (III) chloride.

items.ask: Write the chemical name for MgO: magnesium ___
items.why:
Magnesium (the metal) is named first.
Oxygen (the non-metal) becomes oxide.
Answer: magnesium oxide.

items.text: Write the chemical name for FeS.
items.why:
Iron has two valences, so the name needs a Roman numeral.
One S has valence 2.
One Fe must match it, so iron has valence 2.
Write iron (II), then sulfur → sulfide.
Answer: iron (II) sulfide. The numeral goes right after iron.

items.ask: Write the chemical name for AgCl: silver ___
items.why:
Ag is silver, the metal: it comes first.
Cl is chlorine, the non-metal.
Chlorine changes to chloride.
Answer: silver chloride.

test.why:
Na is sodium, the metal: name it first.
Cl is chlorine: it changes to chloride.
Answer: sodium chloride.
"Sodium chlorine" forgets the -ide ending.

test.text: What is oxygen called in the name of a compound?
test.why:
In a compound the non-metal takes the ending -ide.
Oxygen → oxide (Table 3.5).
Answer: oxide.

Ca is calcium, the metal: name it first.
S is sulfur: it changes to sulfide.
Answer: calcium sulfide.

test.text: How is the ion Fe³⁺ read aloud?
test.why:
Fe³⁺ is iron with valence 3.
It is written iron (III), with a Roman numeral.
It is read "iron three".
Fe²⁺ would be "iron two".

test.text: Name the compound CuO. (O has valence 2.)
test.why:
Copper has more than one valence, so use a Roman numeral.
One O has valence 2.
One Cu must match it, so copper has valence 2.
Answer: copper (II) oxide.
